citation: Photograph of Frances Macbeth Glessner standing in a conservatory among potted plants, full length, in a high-necked gown with puffed sleeves and a ruffled collar, 4 March 1892. Chicago History Museum, ICHi-061818.
author: photographer not named in the museum's record
repository: Chicago History Museum, Images collection, ICHi-061818 (asset 25064; the record gives 2432 x 3128 px as its largest size). The copy used here, 1592 x 2048 px, was supplied by the owner on 2026-11-07 and is held in kevinrhaas/chicago-evidence at evidence/people-portraits-2026-11-07/glessner_frances_m/.
locator: The whole photograph; her face, a three-quarter view turned to her left, is about 90 px across at x 735-825, y 545-680 of the supplied copy.
rights_note: The museum's record marks the image 'No Copyright - United States'; a photograph made in 1892 is out of copyright in the United States. Credit: Chicago History Museum, ICHi-061818.
access_notes: The museum's record (asset 25064) was read on 2026-11-07 (T-3473): it names Frances Macbeth Glessner, gives the date 4 March 1892, and suggests she may be in costume for the Benvenuto Cellini dinner party. The museum's site refuses automated access, so the picture itself was not fetched from it; the owner supplied the copy, and that the copy is ICHi-061818 rests on the owner's identification and the record's description. Nothing else in the record says how she stands.
note: Frances Glessner at 44, standing in a glass-roofed conservatory beside a table of potted chrysanthemums, her right hand at her waist, in a long dark gown with large puffed upper sleeves, a fitted bodice and a high ruffled collar; her hair drawn up and back. Her face is a three-quarter view turned to her left, lit from the front, sharp enough to read the eyes, nose, mouth, chin and right ear.
what_it_supplies: the proportions of Frances Glessner's face (eyes, nose, mouth, chin and ear) as one photograph shows them
how she wore her hair drawn up and back in 1892
what_it_does_not_supply: what she wore day to day: the gown may be a costume, as the museum's record suggests
